name: Pancreas
func: A gland behind the stomach with two jobs: it makes digestive juice full of enzymes and bicarbonate for the duodenum, and its islets release insulin and glucagon to control blood sugar.

levels.kid:
Your **pancreas** is a long, soft gland hiding behind your stomach. It's shaped a bit like a fish lying on its side, with its head tucked into the curve of your intestine and its tail reaching toward your left side.

The pancreas has two big jobs. First, it makes a **digestive juice** full of enzymes that chop food into tiny pieces your body can soak up: sugars, proteins and fats. It squirts that juice into your intestine.

Second, it has tiny islands of special cells that make **insulin**. Insulin is like a key that lets sugar from your food get into your body's cells to give them energy. Without enough insulin, sugar stays stuck in the blood. That's what happens in **diabetes**.
levels.hs:
The **pancreas** is about **12–15 cm** long and lies **retroperitoneally**, across the back of the upper abdomen at about **L1–L2**, behind the stomach and the **lesser sac**.

Its parts, from right to left:
- **Head**: nestled in the C-shaped curve of the **duodenum**. A hook-like extension, the **uncinate process**, curls behind the **superior mesenteric vessels**. The **common bile duct** runs through or behind the head.
- **Neck**: lies in front of the **superior mesenteric vein** and the start of the **portal vein**.
- **Body**: crosses the **aorta**, left kidney and adrenal; the **splenic artery** runs wavily along its upper border, and the **splenic vein** runs in a groove behind it.
- **Tail**: reaches the **hilum of the spleen**, within the splenorenal ligament.

The **main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung)** runs the length of the gland and usually joins the common bile duct at the **ampulla of Vater**, opening at the major duodenal papilla. An **accessory duct (of Santorini)** may open at the minor papilla.

Two functions in one gland:
- **Exocrine** (about 98% of its mass): makes about 1.5 litres a day of **pancreatic juice** containing digestive **enzymes** and **bicarbonate**.
- **Endocrine** (1–2%): the **islets of Langerhans** secrete **insulin** and **glucagon** into the blood to control blood glucose.
levels.college:
**Blood supply**: the head is supplied by the **superior** (from the gastroduodenal artery, coeliac trunk) and **inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries** (from the SMA), forming arcades shared with the duodenum. The body and tail are supplied by **pancreatic branches of the splenic artery**, including the **dorsal pancreatic** and **great pancreatic** (arteria pancreatica magna) arteries. Venous blood drains to the splenic, superior mesenteric and portal veins, so islet hormones reach the **liver first**, a key target of insulin and glucagon.

**Exocrine structure**: **acinar cells** are packed with **zymogen granules** containing inactive enzyme precursors (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase), plus active **amylase** and **lipase**. **Centroacinar** and **duct cells** secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.

**Regulation**: **secretin** (from duodenal S cells, triggered by acid) stimulates bicarbonate and water; **CCK** (I cells, triggered by fat and protein) and **vagal acetylcholine** stimulate enzyme secretion.

**Endocrine islets** (about 1 million, more concentrated in the tail):
- **β cells** (about 60–70% in humans): **insulin** and amylin.
- **α cells** (about 20%): **glucagon**.
- **δ cells**: **somatostatin** (local brake).
- **PP cells**: pancreatic polypeptide; **ε cells**: ghrelin.

**Embryology**: the pancreas forms from **dorsal and ventral buds** of the foregut. The ventral bud rotates with the bile duct behind the duodenum and fuses with the dorsal bud. The ventral bud forms the uncinate process and part of the head; failure of the ducts to fuse produces **pancreas divisum** (the commonest variant), and abnormal rotation can create an **annular pancreas** around the duodenum.

**Nerves**: vagal parasympathetic and coeliac sympathetic fibres. Pancreatic pain is felt in the epigastrium and classically **bores through to the back**.
levels.phd:
**Protection from self-digestion**: enzymes are stored as inactive **zymogens** in granules, together with **SPINK1** (a trypsin inhibitor). Activation normally happens only in the duodenum, when **enteropeptidase** cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which activates the rest. Trypsin can also degrade itself (autolysis) and is inactivated by **chymotrypsin C**. In **pancreatitis**, trypsinogen is activated prematurely inside acinar cells (via cathepsin B, after abnormal calcium signalling and fusion of zymogen granules with lysosomes), triggering autodigestion and inflammation. Gain-of-function mutations in **PRSS1** (cationic trypsinogen) cause **hereditary pancreatitis**; mutations in **SPINK1** and **CFTR** raise risk.

**Bicarbonate secretion** by duct cells: secretin raises cAMP, opening **CFTR** channels, which secrete chloride and bicarbonate, and the **SLC26A6** exchanger trades chloride for bicarbonate, reaching juice concentrations of about **140 mmol/L**. In **cystic fibrosis**, CFTR failure thickens secretions, blocking ducts and destroying the exocrine gland, often from before birth.

**Insulin secretion**: glucose enters β cells via **GLUT** transporters (mainly GLUT1 in humans, GLUT2 in rodents), and **glucokinase**, the "glucose sensor", phosphorylates it. Metabolism raises the **ATP/ADP** ratio, closing **K_ATP channels** (Kir6.2/SUR1), depolarising the cell and opening voltage-gated calcium channels, triggering insulin granule release. Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify this via cAMP. Mutations in Kir6.2 cause **neonatal diabetes**, which can respond to sulfonylurea tablets instead of insulin, a striking example of precision medicine.

**Type 1 diabetes**: autoimmune T-cell destruction of β cells, with autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin) appearing years earlier. **Type 2 diabetes**: insulin resistance plus progressive β-cell dysfunction.

**Research**: stem-cell-derived islets and islet transplantation, β-cell regeneration, and the role of **KRAS** mutations, present in over 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas.
levels.expert:
**Acute pancreatitis**: sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by sitting forward, with vomiting. Diagnosis needs two of: typical pain, serum **lipase** (or amylase) above **three times the upper limit of normal**, and characteristic imaging. Main causes: **gallstones**, high triglycerides, high calcium, ERCP and some medicines. Rare signs of haemorrhagic pancreatitis are **Grey Turner's sign** (flank bruising) and **Cullen's sign** (periumbilical bruising). Severity is graded with scores like the **revised Atlanta classification**, **Glasgow-Imrie** and BISAP. Complications: **necrosis**, infected necrosis, **pseudocysts** (after about 4 weeks), splenic vein thrombosis and **ARDS**. Treatment in general terms: fluids, pain control, early feeding, and treating the cause.

**Chronic pancreatitis**: recurrent pain, **steatorrhoea** (pale, oily, floating stools from fat malabsorption, when over about 90% of exocrine function is lost) and **diabetes**. CT shows **calcifications**; **faecal elastase** is low.

**Pancreatic cancer** (ductal adenocarcinoma): head tumours cause **painless obstructive jaundice** with a palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier's law**), weight loss, and new-onset diabetes. **Trousseau's sign of malignancy**: migratory superficial thrombophlebitis. CT with a pancreatic protocol stages it; **CA 19-9** tracks it. Only about 15–20% are resectable at diagnosis; the operation is the **Whipple procedure** (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for head tumours or **distal pancreatectomy** for body and tail tumours.

**Neuroendocrine tumours**: **insulinoma** (**Whipple's triad**: symptoms of low glucose, measured low glucose, relief when glucose is given; neuroglycopenia can cause confusion, seizures or odd behaviour mistaken for neurological disease), **gastrinoma** (Zollinger–Ellison), glucagonoma and VIPoma. They're part of **MEN1** (pituitary, parathyroid, pancreas).

**Trauma**: the pancreas can be crushed against the spine in seatbelt or handlebar injuries.

keyPoints: Retroperitoneal gland at L1–L2: head, neck, body, tail
Head sits in the duodenal C; tail reaches the spleen
Exocrine: enzymes + bicarbonate via the duct of Wirsung
Endocrine islets: β cells (insulin), α cells (glucagon)
Gallstones are a top cause of acute pancreatitis
Painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder: pancreatic head cancer

test.explain: β cells make insulin; α cells make glucagon; δ cells make somatostatin.

test.q: The enzyme in the duodenum that activates trypsinogen is ______.
test.explain: Enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other zymogens.

test.q: Which artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas?
test.explain: The splenic artery runs a wavy course along the upper border of the body and tail.

test.q: Which lab result supports acute pancreatitis?
choices: Lipase above 3× the upper limit of normal
test.explain: Lipase (or amylase) above three times normal is one of the diagnostic criteria.

test.q: The common anatomical variant where the pancreatic ducts fail to fuse is pancreas ______.
test.explain: In pancreas divisum, most juice drains through the minor papilla via the dorsal duct.

test.q: Which triad defines an insulinoma's hypoglycaemia?
test.explain: Whipple's triad: low-glucose symptoms, measured low glucose, and relief when glucose is given.
